rashi:a1.1: And Rav Anan: who was uncertain in which case the sale is retracted and in which it is not. He had not heard that baraita, which says that a bill of manumission is required; and from what Shmuel said, “it is not sold,” he could not learn anything, for from where [do we know] that “it is not sold” means the money is returned? Perhaps the money the buyer gave the seller is a gift in the seller’s hand. And the difference between Rav and Shmuel is what I explained above.
rashi:a1.2: And the money is returned: for a person knows that betrothal does not take effect with his sister, so he resolved to give it as a deposit; and according to Shmuel, he resolved to give it as a gift.
rashi:a2.1: That you penalize the buyer: in the case of one who sells his slave outside the Land, where we say that the sale is not retracted, and the slave goes free and the buyer loses.
rashi:a2.2: Let us penalize the seller: so that the money is returned and the seller sets him free.
rashi:a3.1: It is not the mouse that steals: a mouse that steals and puts the item away; had it no hole in which to put it, it would not steal. Therefore it is the hole that steals. So too here: had he not found a buyer, he would not have sold him.
rashi:a3.2: The hole, from where would it have it: from where would the hole have the stolen item?
rashi:a3.3: Where the prohibited item is: that is, the buyer, with whom the slave is.
rashi:a5.1: [Give him its value: meaning, the value of the plowing. It teaches us that this is not so.]
rashi:a6.1: That he should not say: the seller, who comes to redeem it at the end of two years, [should not say]: Leave it before me full of produce, the way I left it before you when I sold it to you.
rashi:a6.2: According to the number of years of the crops: this implies all the crops of two years, since [otherwise] it could have written “the number of years” or “the number of crops,” which would have implied two crops.
rashi:a7.1: Mishna. He calculates only: the seller, when he comes to redeem it, [calculates] only with the first. He calculates how many years there were from when he sold it to him until the Jubilee Year, and calculates how much of the maneh falls to each year; and according to that calculation the buyer deducts for him for each year in which he ate [its produce], and he returns the rest to him.
rashi:a7.2: [To the man] to whom he sold it: “And he returns the remainder to the man…” is written of one who redeems a field that he sold.
rashi:a8.1: To the man who is in it: and in the Gemara it asks: From where do we know that we expound it as a leniency? Let us expound it as a stringency.
rashi:a9.1: He may not sell a distant field: which he has, in order to redeem this one, which is near him. The Gemara explains from where we know this.
rashi:a9.2: And he may not borrow: money in order to redeem it.
rashi:a9.3: Permitted in all of them: one who consecrates his field is permitted to sell another field, or to borrow, in order to redeem it. And he redeems by halves: if he does not have enough to redeem all of it, he redeems half of it, and when he is able, he redeems all of it.
rashi:a12.1: Gemara. And it appreciated: on its own.
rashi:a12.2: The remainder in his hand: what remains in his hand of the money he received, after the buyer deducts for him the amount due for each year in which he ate.
rashi:a13.1: Depreciated: it was spoiled and its value dropped.
rashi:a13.2: That is in the land: the remainder, what the land is worth beyond the amount due by the calculation the buyer deducts for him for the years in which he ate. For this word “remainder” can be expounded this way and that way.
rashi:a14.1: What is the difference between them: between Rabbi and Rabbi Dostai, since in any case, according to both of them, we go toward leniency.
rashi:a14.2: Such as where it went up, went down and went up: he sold it to him for two hundred, and the first sold it to the second for a maneh, and it went up in value in the second’s hand and stood at two hundred. According to Rabbi, who said “to the man who is in it,” he gives only a maneh, as much as the second gave for it. According to Rabbi Dostai, he gives two hundred: for if you say “the remainder in his hand,” he took two hundred from the first; and if you say “the remainder in the land,” it is worth two hundred.
rashi:a16.1: Redemption, redemption: it is written here (Leviticus 25:26), “and finds sufficient means for its redemption,” and it is written of a Hebrew slave (ibid. 25:48), “he shall have redemption.”
rashi:a17.1: Only from a maneh: when he comes to redeem himself, he calculates how many years [there are] from the time he was sold (until the Jubilee Year), and calculates how much of that maneh falls to each year; and if two or three years have passed, his master deducts for him according to the amount due for each year, as it is written: “According to the time of a hired worker shall he be with him.”
rashi:a18.1: According to his years: this implies according to the years in which he stands, that is, according to what he is worth at that time.
rashi:a19.1: I have only, etc.: for this verse is written about one sold to a gentile, as it is written (ibid.): “And if a stranger or settler becomes rich…”
rashi:a19.2: Hired worker, hired worker: it is written here (ibid.), “According to the time of a hired worker shall he be with him,” and it is written of one sold to a Jew (Deuteronomy 15:18), “For double the hire of a hired worker he served you…”
rashi:b1.1: I am: praiseworthy in my place, an expounder and expert like ben Azzai, who would praise himself in the markets of Tiberias, as it is taught in Bekhorot, in the ninth chapter (58a): Ben Azzai says: All the Sages of Israel are before me like the peel of garlic.
rashi:b1.2: They can be expounded: these verses of the Hebrew slave.
rashi:b2.1: Kibbar: (Rashi adds an Old French gloss).
rashi:b3.1: From [the statement of] Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Ḥanina: for certainly he came to this only because he was wicked and traded in Sabbatical-Year produce.
rashi:b3.2: The dust of the Sabbatical Year: one who trades in Sabbatical-Year produce. It is called “dust” because this is not the core of the Sabbatical-Year prohibition.
rashi:b4.1: And next to it, “And if you sell something”: and we expound juxtapositions. This is what the Merciful One said: If you do not keep the mitzvot of the Jubilee, in the end you will sell movables and household utensils.
rashi:b5.1: He did not feel: he was not shaken to turn back from the transgression.
rashi:b6.1: It did not come to his hand: this implies that it does not even enter his mind that he is committing any transgression.
rashi:b7.1: It becomes to him as permitted: it seems in his eyes like something permitted. Therefore, in the first clause, where he has so far transgressed only once, it teaches “he did not feel,” which implies that he knew and took to heart that he was transgressing, but did not recoil from the transgression and did it. And the second time it teaches “it did not come to his hand,” that it does not even rise in his mind that it is a transgression.
rashi:b9.1: A person prefers to sell his daughter and not to borrow with interest: interest is written in this passage, as it is written (Leviticus 25:36), “Take no interest or increase from him…”; and certainly before this he had already sold his daughter, since he prefers that.
rashi:b9.2: The redemption of his daughter keeps decreasing: for an ordinary sale of a daughter is only for her to be a maidservant until her days of young womanhood arrive. If he comes to redeem her in the meantime, he calculates how much of the money for which he sold her falls to each year she was to be in the master’s hand, and according to that yearly amount the master deducts for him for each year that she served him, as it is taught in Kiddushin (11a): “Then he shall let her be redeemed” (Exodus 21:8) teaches that she deducts from her redemption payment and goes free.
rashi:b11.1: And becomes a servant: who would become a servant to idol worship, to chop wood and draw water.
rashi:b12.1: He said to him: Abaye [said] to that Sage: Even so, the verse brought him back, so that they should have mercy on him.
rashi:b12.2: Should I throw a stone: that is, that he should never be redeemed.
rashi:b12.3: We will be stringent: with him, so that if he was sold for a maneh and appreciated, he is calculated at two hundred; or if he was sold for two hundred and depreciated, he is calculated at two hundred, as it is written (ibid.), “from the money of his purchase.”
rashi:b14.1: Are there many years: that one year should be longer than another, so that the verse says “if there are yet many in the years,” or a year shorter than another?
rashi:b14.2: Rather: this is what the verse says: If there is an increase in his money in the years in which he stands, that is, he appreciated, he returns his redemption “from the money of his purchase,” for one calculates only by what he was sold for. And if his money remained little in the years in which he stands, e.g., he depreciated, he returns his redemption “according to his years.”
rashi:b15.1: But say: this is what the verse says: Where he served him two years and four remain until the Jubilee, let him give him as much as falls to four years “from the money of his purchase,” according to the calculation by which he bought him.
rashi:b15.2: According to his years: according to the years he still owed to serve him; and the verse does not speak of depreciation and appreciation at all.
rashi:b19.1: And finds another, and he dies: where his fellow was present there at the time this one raised the ax, he is liable [to exile]; excluding one who introduces himself, for whom this one is exempt from exile.
rashi:b20.1: Just as “his hand attains” is now: for certainly at first, when he sold it, his hand did not attain, as it is written (ibid.): “If your brother becomes poor and sells part of his ancestral land.”
rashi:b21.1: “And if the one who consecrates will indeed redeem…” teaches that he borrows: from another and redeems, and if he wishes, he redeems by halves.
rashi:b22.1: His power was diminished: as we said above.
tosafot:a1.1: Perhaps it is not sold and the money is a gift, just as with one who betroths his sister: However, according to the truth, which we have proven, that the money is returned, we say that it is not like one who betroths his sister. For a person knows that betrothal does not take effect with his sister, and resolves to give it as a gift; but with one who sells his field in the Jubilee Year, people are not expert in this, and he did not resolve [to give it] as a gift.
tosafot:a9.1: He may not sell [a field] far away and redeem [one] nearby: the same is true in reverse; it simply states the usual way of things.
tosafot:a14.1: The difference between them is where it went up, went down and went up: it could equally have said “where it went up and went down” with only one buyer. For according to Rabbi, who does not expound “the remainder” [this way], but rather [expounds] “to the man to whom he sold it” and “to the man who is in it,” one must redeem it according to the sale, that is, at the high price; and according to Rabbi Dostai son of Rabbi Yehuda [so Tosafot; the Gemara reads “ben Yehuda”], we go by the value of the land, and it is redeemed according to its value. But since the mishna speaks of two sellers, it preferred to state the difference between them with two sellers as well.
tosafot:b2.1: As it is taught: “Because he fares well with you”: so it appears in all the books, but it seems that we should not read it so, for this is only a narration of the slave’s words, “because he loves you and your house, because he fares well with you,” and it is not a command. Rather, read as it appears in the Sifrei: “As a hired worker, as a settler, he shall be with you” [Leviticus 25:40], which is a command.
tosafot:b3.1: How severe is the dust of the Sabbatical Year: meaning, this is trading, which is not the main prohibition; the main prohibition is plowing and sowing. And if you ask: From where do we know that these misfortunes explained here come upon him through trading alone? Perhaps they come only through plowing and sowing? One can say that this is measure for measure: because he sold Sabbatical-Year produce, he sells what is his.
tosafot:b11.1: Or to the offshoot [le’eker]: this is one who is sold to idol worship itself. It expounds it so because the end of idolatries is to be uprooted [le’akker].
tosafot:b15.1: But say: where he served two and four remain, etc.: Rashi explained that the verse does not speak of depreciation and appreciation at all. But this does not seem right to me, for if so, this would be nothing but the plain sense of the verse, and we would learn it without the superfluous word, whereas it implies that Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak derives it from the superfluous word. Therefore it seems right to explain: But say: where he served two and four remain, let him give him four “from the money of his purchase,” whether he depreciated or appreciated; and where he served four and two remain, let him give him two “according to his years,” whether he depreciated or appreciated. And for this the superfluous word of the verse comes: that we always go by the nearer one.
gershom:a1.1: (For from where [do we know] that it is not sold and the money is returned? Perhaps…)
gershom:a2.1: This baraita, that he requires a bill of manumission from his second master, he had not heard.
gershom:a3.1: From Shmuel’s statement too one cannot learn that the sale is retracted, for from where [do we know] that “it is not sold” means the money is returned? Perhaps it is not sold and the money is a gift, which is not returned, just as with one who betroths his sister, where Rav says the money is returned, since betrothal does not take effect with his sister.
gershom:a4.1: And Shmuel says the money is a gift: for a person knows that betrothal does not take effect with his sister, and he resolved to give it to her as a gift. [And if you ask:] Now, since you said that according to Shmuel the money is a gift, which is not returned to the buyer, then this is Rav’s view; what is the difference between them? The difference between them is where the buyer seized [the field] and ate produce: according to Rav, who said it is sold, he does not pay for the produce; according to Shmuel, who said it is not sold, he pays for the produce.
gershom:a5.1: What did you see that we penalize the buyer?
gershom:a6.1: Who acquired him outside the Land: that he must set him free and lose his money.
gershom:a7.1: Let us penalize the seller: anyone who sold him [to a buyer] outside the Land.
gershom:a8.1: The hole steals: that is, the one who buys causes this one to take him out of the Land and sell him.
gershom:a9.1: Where the prohibited item is: he is in the buyer’s hand, so we penalize him; therefore we penalize the buyer.
gershom:a10.1: Is it necessary [to state] that he plowed: that it counts for him, since he already did some work in it?
gershom:a11.1: Plowed was necessary: that it counts for him. For you might have said: since he plowed and did not sow, and the buyer derived no benefit from it, we say to the seller when he redeems: since this one troubled himself with it, plowing and improving it, and had no benefit from it, give the buyer the value of his improvement, since he plowed and improved it.
gershom:a12.1: And let him leave: that is, when he returns to him the remainder of the money for the years still left until the Jubilee, and the value of his plowing and of the improvement he made, and afterward he withdraws and goes out of the field.
gershom:a13.1: It teaches us: that the seller gives him nothing for the plowing, for he says to him: Since it was in your possession, and you could have sown it and taken its crop, and you did not, you are the one who caused yourself a loss. And the seller deducts the value of those two years as if they had been sown and the buyer had eaten their crop.
gershom:a14.1: From where [do we know] that the seller should not say to the buyer: Leave the field before me full of produce at the end of the two years, so that you do not take its produce, the way I left it before you full when I sold it to you?
gershom:a15.1: The verse states: “According to the number of years of the crops he shall sell to you”: that is, all the crops that can be in it from the time of the sale to the end of two years are sold and belong to the buyer.
gershom:a16.1: He sold his field to the first for a maneh, and the first buyer then sold it to the second for two hundred; when the seller, who is the owner of the field, redeems it:
gershom:a17.1: He calculates only: as it is written: “And he calculates the years of its sale and returns the remainder.”
gershom:a18.1: Only with the first: to whom he sold it, so as to make it easier for the redeemer, and the second buyer loses one maneh. And likewise, if he sold it to the first for two hundred and the buyer then sold it to the second for a maneh, the one who was owner of the field, when he comes to redeem it, calculates only with the last buyer.
gershom:a19.1: As it is stated: “And he returns the remainder to the man”: [to the man who is in it], that is, to the one who holds the field. We expound the verse this way because we wish to make it easier for the redeemer; but in that [other] way we would be stringent with the redeemer.
gershom:a20.1: That he may not sell [a field] far away [and redeem one nearby: that is, if the redeemer has a field far from him, he is not permitted to sell it in order to redeem with that money this field, which is near him, which he sold for two crop-years; and in the Gemara we explain the reason. And likewise he may not sell a bad field that he has in order to redeem with that money a good field of his that he sold for two crop-years. And likewise he is not permitted to borrow money from another to redeem this field, and he is not permitted to redeem it by halves, unless he gives all the money at once.]
gershom:a21.1: And with consecrated property: one who consecrates his field when the Jubilee is in effect is permitted in all of them: to sell a distant field and redeem a near one, [to sell] a bad one [and redeem a good one], [to borrow and redeem], and to redeem by halves. And although we said above that if he says, “I will give the amount year by year,” we do not listen to him, that is only that we do not listen to him [to redeem it] by giving a sela and a pundeyon each year; but if he gives half [together] and later the other half, it is permitted. And this is what it says: with consecrated property it is permitted to redeem by halves.
gershom:a22.1: The remainder in his hand: that is, the remainder in the seller’s hand of the money the buyer gave him [he returns to the buyer], and not the improvement by which it improved.
gershom:a23.1: The remainder in the land: that is, for we go toward leniency with the [redeemer; the printed text reads “priest”].
gershom:a24.1: What is the difference between them: [between Rabbi and Rabbi Dostai], since both of them are lenient with the redeemer?
gershom:a25.1: The difference between them is where it went up, went down and went up: that is, he sold it to him for two hundred and it went down [that is, it depreciated], and at the time of redemption it went up and was worth two hundred. According to Rabbi, who speaks neither of the remainder in his hand nor of the remainder in the land nor of depreciation, [by his reasoning,] if he sold it for two hundred and it went down [that is, depreciated] and then stood again at two hundred [that is, appreciated], and there is only one buyer, we say he redeems it for two hundred [that is, “to the man to whom he sold it”]. And according to Rabbi Dostai, who goes by the remainder in his hand and the remainder in the land, we also go by the land, so it is calculated for him at the lower value.
gershom:a26.1: [And some say: according to Rabbi, who goes by the land, since at the time of redemption it is worth as much as at the time of sale, he gives him two hundred, as at the time of sale.] And from where [do we know] that it is for leniency? Say for stringency: that is, the verses can be expounded [as a leniency for the redeemer, and they can be expounded] as a stringency. For one could say: when the first sold it to the second for two hundred, from where [do we know] that he calculates only with the second? The verse states “to the man who is in it,” and that is a stringency. And when [he sold it] to the first for two hundred, from where [do we know] that he calculates only with the first? The verse states “to the man to whom he sold it,” and that is a stringency. So from where do we know to expound them as a leniency?
gershom:a27.1: For he derives “redemption,” “redemption” from a Hebrew slave: it is written here, “And he prospers and finds sufficient means for its redemption,” and it is written of a Hebrew slave, “According to them he shall return the price of his redemption.”
gershom:a28.1: From the money of his purchase: from where [do we know] that he calculates only from a maneh, that he also deducts the value of the years of his service and gives the balance for the years remaining until the seventh year? As it is stated, “from the money of his purchase”: he calculates from the time he was sold. “According to his years”: what he is worth now. And these verses speak of a Hebrew slave sold to a gentile.
gershom:a29.1: Hired worker, hired worker, for a verbal analogy: it is written here, of one sold to a Jew, “As a hired worker, as a settler, he shall be with you,” and it is written here, of one sold to a gentile, “As a hired worker year by year.”
gershom:b1.1: I am like ben Azzai in the markets of Tiberias: just as he was a great Sage who would stand in the market and say, “Whoever wishes to ask me anything, I will answer him,” so too I: whoever wishes, let him come and ask me.
gershom:b2.1: [Now, these verses of a Hebrew slave can be expounded both as a leniency and as a stringency.] As a stringency: one could say, when he appreciated, from where [do we know] that he calculates only at two hundred? The verse states “according to his years.” And if he depreciated, from where [do we know] that he calculates only at two hundred? The verse states “from the money of his purchase.” And that is as a stringency.
gershom:b3.1: Since the Merciful One was lenient with him: that one may not treat him in a degrading manner, He was also lenient with his redemption.
gershom:b4.1: The dust of the Sabbatical Year: “dust” as in a whiff of the Sabbatical-Year prohibition. That is, the main prohibition of the Sabbatical Year is one who hoards Sabbatical-Year produce until the shemitta, whereas trading in Sabbatical-Year produce is not the main prohibition of the Sabbatical Year; we only expound the verse, “for eating” and not for trading. Even so, that sin causes him to sell his movables, as it is written, “And if you sell something”: the vav [“and”] adds to the previous matter, [teaching] that this sale comes because of the sin of selling Sabbatical-Year produce. He did not feel: that he did not regret it, but went back and sold more.
gershom:b5.1: It did not come to his hand: that is, since he repeated the transgression, it seems to him as permitted, and he does not set his heart to return in repentance; [that is “it did not come to his hand.” And even though his daughter is not written in this passage, a person prefers: that is, it is better for him to sell his daughter before he borrows with interest. For his daughter, if her hand attains so that she redeems herself, or another of her relatives redeems her, deducts from her redemption payment and goes free, like a Hebrew slave, where one deducts the years of her servitude from her price; whereas one who borrows with interest adds the interest on top of the principal and pays it.]
gershom:b6.1: Not to you, but to a stranger: that is, [at times] he does not merit to be sold to you, but to a stranger, which is a great degradation, that he serves a stranger.
gershom:b7.1: To a ger toshav: who is not a convert in every respect, but only renounces idol worship.
gershom:b8.1: This is one sold to idol worship itself: that he sweeps and sprinkles [the floor] before it; and that is le’eker, that he is uprooted for the needs of idol worship. And since he caused himself to be sold through the sin of trading in Sabbatical-Year produce, we will be still more stringent with him, and when he is redeemed his hand will be the lower.
gershom:b9.1: He said to him: But the verse brought him back, for the verse had mercy on him afterward, as the verse says, “he shall have redemption,” and “in the Jubilee he shall go out,” after he was sold. And since the verse brought him back and had mercy on him [the text here is garbled; a marginal note reads “and had mercy on him”], therefore when he is redeemed, too, it has mercy on him and his hand is the upper.
gershom:b10.1: And are there many years or few years in one Sabbatical cycle more than in another? Rather, this is its meaning: if his money increased in the years of his service, e.g., he appreciated, when he is redeemed one calculates by the money of his purchase, as it is written, “If there are yet many in the years, according to them he shall return the price of his redemption from the money of his purchase.”
gershom:b11.1: And if his money decreased: e.g., he depreciated, he gives according to [the years], “according to his years,” as he is worth now; that is, “And if there remain but few in the years…” And from here we learn explicitly that he is redeemed and his hand is the upper.
gershom:b12.1: But say [these verses come for this]: where he served two [years of the seven and four more years remain, and he redeems himself, he gives his owner the value of four years] “from the money of his purchase,” which was given for him. That is, “if there are yet many in the years”: he served less than half of the seven, so he gives him the value of four years according to the calculation by which he bought him. And “if there remain but few in the years” is where he served four and two remain, and now he is redeemed, he gives him the value of two years; and that is “according to his years,” that is, according to the few years that remain. For this they come, and not to be lenient with him as you expounded.
gershom:b13.1: If so: that they come for this, let it write, “if there are yet many years.”
gershom:b14.1: What is “in the years”? Conclude from it that if his money increased in the years, that he appreciated, he gives “from the money of his purchase,” to be lenient, as we said.
gershom:b15.1: Like Sinai: that this is their meaning.
gershom:b16.1: He may not sell far away, etc.: as we explained above.
gershom:b17.1: “And his hand attains”: his own hand; that is, if he attained from his own [means], and not that he borrows.
gershom:b18.1: And finds: after he sold; excluding what was available, that he may not sell what he had before that, e.g., he may not sell far away, etc.
gershom:b19.1: Sufficient means to redeem it: that is, if he attained enough to redeem all of it at once, he redeems, and he is not permitted to redeem by halves.
gershom:b20.1: Is this to say: that “and finds,” written in “and his hand attains and finds,” implies now, that is, that he found after he sold?
gershom:b21.1: “And finds another and he dies,” and he is a victim of circumstance, for [the other] was already present; excluding one who introduced himself, for then he is exempt.
gershom:b22.1: Just as “and his hand attains” implies after he sold, for had it attained at the time of sale, he would not have sold.
gershom:b23.1: So too “and finds” also implies now, after he sold. And with consecrated property he is permitted in all of them, to sell, etc. (And we do not read “in the sacred.”) And so all of them: “This is a stringency with an ordinary person over consecrated property,” that he is permitted to do all of these to take it out of the hand of the Temple treasury.
gershom:b24.1: His power was diminished: in that he does not borrow and redeem, as we said.
gershom:b25.1: [But] with one who consecrates an ancestral field: since his power was diminished in another respect, his power was enhanced in this one respect; therefore with consecrated property he is permitted in all of them.
